newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists, Communists seek election pact.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists, Communists seek election pact.

text.p: The leaders of France's opposition Socialist and Communist parties hope to seal a pre-election rapprochement when they meet next Tuesday despite persistent differences over a single European currency.
Lionel Jospin and Robert Hue are to meet at a neutral, but not yet agreed, venue to close ranks for the snap parliamentary election called for May 25 and June 1 by President Jacques Chirac.

They are likely to issue a joint declaration of intention to govern together if the Left wins the election, but Hue stressed on Thursday they were not negotiating a detailed "common programme" such as the two parties drafted in the 1970s.

Jospin made a significant gesture towards the Communists this week when he ruled out a further wave of austerity to prepare France for European economic and monetary union (EMU) and said the deficit limit criterion set in the Maastricht Treaty should not be applied dogmatically.
Hue welcomed what he called this positive evolution in the Socialist position.

"I am delighted that the Socialist Party no longer makes the convergence criteria for a single currency a condition for the Left's policy, since our social proposals are in opposition to the single currency," he told the newspaper Le Figaro.
"Each party will enter the election with its own programme. What we hope is to identify some broad guidelines which would serve as joint commitments towards our people for a new policy," Hue said.

He said his party was no longer obsessed with "the cult of nationalisation", but he said it seemed obvious that France's two biggest water companies, Generale des Eaux and Lyonnaise des Eaux, should be nationalised.
Hue has said Communist ministers should serve in a coalition government, but Socialist officials said that would depend on agreement on policy.

Four Communists served in Socialist-led administrations under the late president Francois Mitterrand from 1981, but they were given little say in economic or foreign policy and quit in 1984 after the Socialists turned towards fiscal austerity.
Socialist negotiators say the Communists, who are demanding a referendum before France joins the euro common currency, have eased their overall hostility towards European integration.

However, Jospin is prepared to promise only a parliamentary vote -- not a referendum -- on EMU. He argues that French voters have already approved the single currency in a 1992 referendum which narrowly approved the Maastricht treaty.
"It wouldn't have been possible for the Socialist Party to accept a summit meeting if the Communist Party had not claritied its position on Europe." one Socialist negotiator said.
"The Communists have moved from 'no Europe' to demanding 'a different Europe', which puts them within the European framework," he said.
Addressing a Communist forum on Europe in the northern town of Douai on Thursday, politburo member Francis Wurtz signalled a slight easing of the party's hostility to monetary union.
He called for a "transformed European monetary system" based on the European Currency Unit (ECU) as "an instrument of monetary cooperation between sovereign nations and partners".
The ECU, Wurtz said, should be "a common, not a single currency, based on national currencies".
